If a practitioner judges combined use necessary, it should only be by an experienced TCM physician using well-processed material, prolonged pre-decoction of the aconite, controlled herb ratios, and monitoring for cardiac/neurologic toxicity.

sources.note: Journal of Ethnopharmacology 2024, DOI 10.1016/j.jep.2024.118212. Rat PK study: Pinellia enhances absorption of aconitine and benzoylaconine and alters CYP-enzyme-mediated metabolism of toxic Aconitum alkaloids; concludes the incompatibility mechanism is linked to increased in vivo exposure to toxic compounds. Fetched and read PubMed page.

Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine 2018, DOI 10.1155/2018/2875873, PMC6146551. Animal study: Fuzi+Banxia combination aggravated adriamycin cardiomyopathy, increased cardiac cell death, prolonged QT/QTc, and abolished PKA/beta2AR-Gs cardioprotection seen with single herbs. Fetched and read PMC page.

Chinese Medicine 2021, DOI 10.1186/s13020-021-00472-9, PMC8314510. Review explicitly lists Banxia (Pinelliae rhizome) among herbs classically incompatible with Aconitum and notes cardiotoxicity increases when processed Fuzi (Heishunpian) is combined with these herbs; does not detail a hydrolysis mechanism. Fetched and read PMC page.

mechanism: Fritillaria (Beimu) alkaloids inhibit intestinal P-glycoprotein, an efflux transporter. Benzoylmesaconine and related diester/monoester aconite alkaloids from Aconitum are P-gp substrates, so blocking efflux lets more of the toxic alkaloid cross the gut wall and reach the circulation. The toxic load is not raised during co-decoction but during intestinal absorption, so the combined preparation delivers a higher systemic dose of aconite's cardiotoxic alkaloids.
clinical_effect: Increased systemic exposure to aconite's cardiotoxic alkaloids, raising the risk of aconitine-type poisoning: palpitations/arrhythmias, paresthesia, nausea, hypotension, and potentially fatal ventricular arrhythmias.
management: Do not co-prescribe. This is a classical Eighteen Incompatibles (十八反) wutou-beimu contraindication and modern data support enhanced aconite absorption, so the pair should be avoided in the same formula. If aconite-type toxicity is suspected after exposure, treat supportively with cardiac monitoring and antiarrhythmic management.

sources.note: Experimental study (Liu, Wei, Kanai, He; Evid Based Complement Alternat Med 2021;2021:8351717; DOI 10.1155/2021/8351717). Fritillaria alkaloids inhibit intestinal P-gp; benzoylmesaconine from prepared aconite is a P-gp substrate, so co-administration increases intestinal absorption/permeability of the toxic aconite alkaloid. Toxicity rises during absorption, not decoction. Provides a modern mechanistic basis for the traditional incompatibility. Fetched and confirmed on PMC8510812 and PubMed.

Review (Chan, Wang, Feng; Chinese Medicine 2021;16:61; DOI 10.1186/s13020-021-00472-9). Confirms Beimu (Fritillaria) is one of the herbs classically regarded as incompatible with Aconitum under the '18 incompatible medicaments' (十八反), and notes that cardiotoxicity of processed Fuzi (Heishunpian) increases when combined with these herbs. Documents the classical contraindication but gives limited pair-specific toxicology. Fetched and confirmed on PMC8314510 and PubMed.

mechanism: This is a classical Chinese-medicine incompatibility from the "Eighteen Incompatibles" (十八反, wutou-gualou pair): aconite and Trichosanthes are traditionally held not to be combined. In modern terms the cited review frames it as opposing herb natures (hot, highly toxic aconitine-bearing aconite versus cold-natured Gualou) and notes that the cardiotoxicity attributed to the diterpenoid alkaloids of processed aconite is reported to rise when it is co-formulated with the five proscribed herbs, of which Gualou is one. The molecular basis for the Gualou pair specifically is not well established; the contraindication itself, not a defined pharmacological pathway, is the sourced fact.
clinical_effect: Potential for enhanced aconite-type toxicity (notably cardiotoxicity such as arrhythmia, plus the usual aconitine neuro/cardiac toxic syndrome) if the two herbs are used together; traditionally the combination is simply avoided.
management: Avoid co-prescribing aconite (Fuzi/Chuanwu/Wutou) with Trichosanthes (Gualou) in the same formula, consistent with the classical 十八反 contraindication. If aconite is used, ensure it is properly processed and correctly dosed, and monitor for signs of aconitine toxicity (paresthesia, nausea, arrhythmia). Defer to a qualified TCM practitioner before combining.

sources.note: Same article verified directly on its PubMed page (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34315520): title, authors (Yau-Tuen Chan, Ning Wang, Yibin Feng), journal Chinese Medicine, year 2021, and DOI 10.1186/s13020-021-00472-9 all confirmed. This is the PMID/DOI for the same source, listed separately to document the verification.

mechanism: Classical 十八反 (Eighteen Incompatibles) counter-pair. In experimental models Veratrum nigrum (lilu) attenuates or reverses Panax ginseng's biological activities (anti-metastatic, estrogenic and neuro-active effects), i.e. it diminishes ginseng's pharmacological action; Veratrum's steroidal alkaloids are themselves highly toxic.
clinical_effect: Loss of ginseng's intended effects when the two are combined; traditionally a forbidden pair. Independent toxicity of Veratrum alkaloids adds risk.
management: Classical 十八反 contraindication - do not combine ginseng with Veratrum. Evidence is experimental (animal/in-vitro) only; no human interaction reports.

sources.note: J Ethnopharmacol 2018 (DOI 10.1016/j.jep.2018.03.036). Explicitly identifies Veratrum nigrum as incompatible with Panax ginseng within the 'Eighteen Incompatible Medicaments'; experimentally, adding Veratrum attenuated ginseng's anti-metastatic effect in vitro and in vivo (pharmacodynamic antagonism / reduced ginseng efficacy).

Sci Rep 2016 (PMCID PMC4882595; DOI 10.1038/srep26924). States the pair is recorded in 'the eighteen incompatible medicaments'; Veratrum attenuated ginseng-induced rises in serum estradiol and ERalpha/ERbeta, i.e., antagonized ginseng's estrogenic activity. Authors call it pharmacological evidence for the doctrine.

J Pharm Biomed Anal 2022 (DOI 10.1016/j.jpba.2021.114442). Calls PG+VN the most representative incompatibility herb pair in TCM; combining the two decreased ginseng's benefit on depression-like behavior, brain neurotransmitters and serum estrogen in OVX rats, with gut-microbiota and metabolite changes. Does not document human clinical adverse events.

mechanism: This is a classical "Eighteen Incompatibles" (十八反) pair: Lilu (Veratrum) is traditionally listed as incompatible with the "shen" herbs, including Danshen. The traditional basis is that pairing the strongly emetic, steroidal-alkaloid-bearing Veratrum with these herbs is unsafe. The one experimental study on this exact pair did not find enhanced acute toxicity but rather an antagonistic pharmacodynamic interaction: Veratrum suppressed estradiol secretion and blunted the upregulation of estrogen receptors alpha and beta that Danshen normally produces, so the two herbs work against each other on the estrogenic axis. Mechanistically that is consistent with the classical idea that combining them yields an unfavorable/counterproductive result rather than a useful one.
clinical_effect: Per classical doctrine the pair is forbidden and should never be co-prescribed. In the available experimental model, Veratrum reduced (antagonized) Danshen's estrogen-like activity on reproductive tissue, an undesirable loss of expected effect; the broader human toxicity feared traditionally has not been formally demonstrated.
management: Treat as an absolute classical contraindication: do not combine Veratrum nigrum (Lilu) with Salvia miltiorrhiza (Danshen) in the same formula. Substitute an appropriate alternative for one of the herbs and consult a qualified TCM practitioner; this restriction is codified in the Chinese Pharmacopoeia tradition.

sources.note: Phytomedicine, 2018; DOI 10.1016/j.phymed.2018.03.038. Fetched the PubMed abstract page. Explicitly frames the SM+VN pair as one of the 18 incompatible medicaments (shibafan) prohibited for thousands of years and provides experimental evidence: in immature/OVX mice and ER-pathway in vitro assays, Veratrum nigrum inhibited Salvia miltiorrhiza's estrogenic activity by interfering with estradiol secretion and suppressing ERalpha/ERbeta upregulation, concluding the combination produces unfavorable effects. Single endpoint, single study — supports the classical contraindication and gives limited (possible-level) experimental backing.

mechanism: Co-decoction of the two herbs lowers the recoverable amount of ginseng's active ginsenosides, so less of ginseng's pharmacologically active material survives into the combined preparation. The chemical interaction during joint extraction (rather than any newly formed toxin) appears to drive the loss of activity. Classically this is framed as Wulingzhi 'counteracting'/restraining ginseng, one of the Nineteen Mutual Fears (十九畏).
clinical_effect: Reduced ginseng effect: lower ginsenoside content and weakened antiplatelet (Qi-tonifying/blood-moving) action of ginseng when the two are decocted together. No toxicity demonstrated in the cited work; the concern is loss of therapeutic efficacy plus traditional contraindication status.
management: Treat as a traditional incompatible/forbidden pair: per the Chinese Pharmacopoeia and the Nineteen Mutual Fears (十九畏), renshen (ginseng) co-prescribed with wulingzhi (Trogopterus dung) is not recommended. However, modern prescription-network data show the pair IS still co-used clinically for blood-stasis-with-Qi-deficiency, so the prohibition is contested; if avoiding co-decoction, separate the herbs in time or substitute, since joint extraction diminishes ginseng's activity.

sources.note: Chemistry & Biodiversity, 2025, Wu et al. (DOI 10.1002/cbdv.202500770). VERIFIED by direct re-fetch: title, journal, year, authors, DOI all match. Abstract names Red Ginseng + Trogopterus Feces as a 'nineteen medicaments of mutual antagonism' pair not recommended in the Chinese Pharmacopoeia; in vitro co-decoction significantly reduced bioactive ginsenoside content and diminished antiplatelet efficacy. No toxicity data. Strongest, most pair-specific source; justifies 'possible' (single in vitro herb-pair study).

Zhongguo Zhong Yao Za Zhi, 2017, Li et al. (DOI 10.19540/j.cnki.cjcmm.2017.0140). VERIFIED by direct re-fetch: title, journal, year, authors, DOI all match. Scale-free complex-network analysis of renshen-Trogopterus Dung prescriptions within the nineteen-mutual-restraint framework; documents the pair is real, studied, and clinically co-prescribed for blood-stasis syndrome - tempers a blanket prohibition.

Evidence-Based Complement Alternat Med, 2013, Long et al. (DOI 10.1155/2013/352145). VERIFIED by direct re-fetch (PubMed + Hindawi): title, journal, year, DOI all match. Concludes the 'eighteen antagonisms and nineteen mutual inhibitors' rule has a discernible chemical/network basis. Supports the rule generally; does NOT name the ginseng-wulingzhi pair specifically (disclosed). Background corroboration only.
